title: Sherlock Holmes: The Red-Headed League
author: Arthur Conan Doyle
ru: Холмс расследует странную работу для рыжих мужчин и раскрывает план ограбления банка

chapters.title: Chapter 1. A Man with Red Hair
chapters.text:
One autumn day I went to visit my friend Sherlock Holmes at his rooms in Baker Street. When I opened the door, I saw that he was talking to a large, elderly gentleman with bright red hair. I wanted to leave, but Holmes pulled me into the room.

“You have come at the perfect time, my dear Watson,” he said. “This is Mr Jabez Wilson. He has just started to tell me a very unusual story. I think you will enjoy it.”

The visitor stood up and nodded to me. He was a fat, slow man in old but clean clothes. His hair was the colour of fire.

Holmes looked at him for a moment and smiled. “Apart from the obvious facts that he has done hard work with his hands, that he takes snuff, that he has been to China and that he has done a lot of writing lately, I know nothing about him.”

Mr Wilson jumped in his chair. “How on earth did you know all that, Mr Holmes?”

“Your right hand is bigger than your left, so you have worked with it. There is a small Chinese fish tattooed on your wrist, and the pink colour of the fish is only done in China. And the cuff of your right sleeve is very shiny from resting on a desk.”

Mr Wilson laughed. “Well, I thought at first that you had done something clever, but I see now that it was simple after all.”

Then he took an old newspaper out of his pocket and gave it to me. “Please read this advertisement, doctor,” he said. “It is where the whole business started.”

I read it aloud:

“TO THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE. There is now another vacancy for a member of the League. The salary is four pounds a week for purely nominal services. All red-headed men over twenty-one years of age are eligible. Apply in person on Monday at eleven o’clock to Duncan Ross, at the offices of the League, 7 Pope’s Court, Fleet Street.”

“What on earth does this mean?” I asked.

Holmes laughed quietly. “It is a little strange, isn’t it? Now, Mr Wilson, tell us everything about yourself and about how this advertisement has changed your life.”

chapters.title: Chapter 2. The Red-Headed League
chapters.text:
“I have a small pawnbroker’s shop in Saxe-Coburg Square, near the City,” Mr Wilson began. “Business has not been good for some years. I have only one assistant, a young man called Vincent Spaulding. He agreed to work for half the usual wages, because he wanted to learn the business.”

“That is very generous of him,” said Holmes.

“Yes, and he is a good worker, although he has one hobby. He loves photography. He is always taking pictures and then running down into the cellar to develop them. But apart from that, he has no faults.

“Eight weeks ago Spaulding came into the office with this newspaper. ‘I wish I had red hair, Mr Wilson,’ he said. ‘There is another job in the League of the Red-Headed Men. It pays very well, and you only have to work a few hours a day.’

“I had never heard of the League, so he explained it to me. A rich American called Ezekiah Hopkins, who had red hair himself, had left all his money to help men with red hair. If I applied, Spaulding said, I would have a good chance, because my hair was so bright.

“So we closed the shop and went to Fleet Street. When we arrived, I could not believe my eyes. The street was full of men with hair of every shade: orange, brick, gold, dark brown. I nearly went home, but Spaulding pushed me through the crowd and up the stairs to the office.

“There was a small man behind a table. His name was Duncan Ross, and his hair was even redder than mine. Then he suddenly took my hair in both hands and pulled it hard until I cried out.

“‘There are tears in your eyes,’ he said, ‘so it is real. We have been tricked twice by men in wigs.’ Then he shook my hand and told me that the job was mine.

“The work was simple. I had to sit in his office from ten until two every day and copy out the Encyclopaedia Britannica by hand. If I left the office even once, I would lose the position forever. My pay was four pounds a week.

“Luckily, my business is busiest in the evenings, and Spaulding said he could look after the shop in the mornings. So I agreed immediately. I have never been happier with a job.”

Holmes rubbed his hands together. “Please continue, Mr Wilson. This is extremely interesting.”

chapters.title: Chapter 3. The League Is Dissolved
chapters.text:
“For eight weeks everything went well,” said Mr Wilson. “Every morning I went to the office at ten and sat at my desk with pens, ink and paper. At first Mr Duncan Ross came in often to check on me, but later he stopped coming. Still, I never left the room, because I did not want to lose the job.

“I copied the articles about Abbots, Archery, Armour and Architecture. I had nearly finished the letter A, and I hoped to start on B soon. Every Saturday Mr Ross paid me four gold coins. It was the easiest money I have ever earned.

“And then, this morning, everything ended. I went to the office at ten o’clock as usual, but the door was locked. There was a small card on it.”

He handed the card to Holmes, who read it out:

“THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE IS DISSOLVED. October 9, 1890.”

Holmes and I looked at the card and at the sad face of our visitor. Suddenly the whole thing seemed so funny that we both burst out laughing.

“I cannot see anything funny!” cried Mr Wilson, and his face went as red as his hair. “If you only want to laugh at me, I will go somewhere else.”

“No, no,” said Holmes, pushing him back into his chair. “I would not miss your case for the world. But you must admit that it is a little unusual. What did you do when you found the card?”

“I asked the landlord on the ground floor. He had never heard of the League or of Duncan Ross. He said the man in that office was a lawyer called William Morris, and he had moved out yesterday. He gave me a new address, but when I went there, I found a factory that made artificial knees. Nobody there knew Mr Morris or Mr Ross.”

“And what did your assistant say?”

“Spaulding told me to wait. He said that perhaps I would get a letter. But I did not want to lose such a good job without a fight, so I came to you.”

“You were right to come,” said Holmes. “I think this may be more serious than it seems. Tell me, how long had Spaulding worked for you before he showed you the advertisement?”

“About a month.”

“Is he a small, strong man, very quick, with no hair on his face and a white mark on his forehead from acid?”

Mr Wilson was very surprised. “Yes, that is him exactly! Do you know him?”

“I have heard of him,” said Holmes quietly. “That is all for today, Mr Wilson. I hope we will have an answer for you by Monday.”

chapters.title: Chapter 4. Saxe-Coburg Square
chapters.text:
When our visitor had left, Holmes sat in his chair with his eyes closed and smoked his pipe for nearly an hour. He called it “a three-pipe problem”. I thought he had fallen asleep, but suddenly he jumped up.

“Come, Watson,” he said. “We are going to Saxe-Coburg Square. After that we will listen to some music. There is a violin concert this afternoon.”

Saxe-Coburg Square was a small, poor, dirty place. On one corner we found a house with three golden balls over the door and the name JABEZ WILSON on a sign. Holmes stood in front of it for some time and looked carefully at the houses. Then he walked up and down the street, and to my surprise he hit the pavement two or three times with his stick. Finally he knocked on the door of the shop.

A young man with a clean face opened it immediately.

“Excuse me,” said Holmes. “Could you tell me the way to the Strand?”

“Third right, fourth left,” the young man answered quickly, and closed the door.

“He is a smart fellow,” said Holmes as we walked away. “I think he is the fourth smartest man in London. I have heard of him before.”

“You clearly wanted to see him,” I said.

“Not him. I wanted to see the knees of his trousers.”

“And what did you see?”

“What I expected to see. And now, my dear doctor, let us look at the other side of the square.”

We turned the corner and found ourselves in a completely different world. This street was one of the busiest in the city. It was full of fine shops and large business buildings. Holmes studied the buildings one by one.

“Let me remember the order of the houses,” he said. “There is the tobacconist, the little newspaper shop, the Coburg branch of the City and Suburban Bank, the vegetarian restaurant and the carriage builder. That is enough. Our work is done. Now for the music!”

All afternoon Holmes sat at the concert and moved his long fingers to the music with a happy, dreamy smile. But on the way home he became serious.

“A terrible crime is being planned, Watson,” he said. “I have every reason to believe that we will be in time to stop it. But today is Saturday, so it will happen tonight. I will need your help. Come to Baker Street at ten o’clock. And bring your army revolver.”

chapters.title: Chapter 5. In the Bank Cellar
chapters.text:
At ten o’clock I arrived at Baker Street. Two men were already there with Holmes. One was Peter Jones, a police detective from Scotland Yard. The other was Mr Merryweather, a director of the City and Suburban Bank. We all got into two carriages and drove through the dark streets.

Mr Merryweather took us through a side door of the bank and down some stone steps into a large cellar. It was full of heavy wooden boxes.

“Thirty thousand French gold coins are here,” he said nervously.

“And now we must sit in the dark and wait,” said Holmes. “The man we are waiting for is John Clay. He is a murderer, a thief and a forger, and he is one of the cleverest criminals in London. He calls himself Vincent Spaulding now.”

Holmes covered the lamp, and we sat in total darkness. The time passed very slowly. After more than an hour, I suddenly saw a thin line of light between the stones in the floor. Then one of the large stones turned over, and a hand appeared. A moment later a young man with a clean face climbed up out of the hole.

“It’s all clear,” he whispered to someone behind him. “Have you got the bags? Great Scott! Jump, Archie, jump!”

Holmes had jumped out and caught him by the collar. The other man, who had red hair, disappeared back into the tunnel, but the police were waiting for him at the other end. Jones quickly put handcuffs on John Clay.

Later that night, at Baker Street, Holmes explained everything to me.

“It was clear from the beginning,” he said, “that the League and the copying of the Encyclopaedia had only one purpose. The criminals wanted to get Mr Wilson out of his shop for a few hours every day. Clay’s partner, with his red hair, played Duncan Ross. Meanwhile Clay dug a tunnel from the cellar of the shop.”

“How did you know it was a tunnel?” I asked.

“His ‘photography’ took him to the cellar every day. When I knocked on the pavement, I learned that the cellar went in front of the house, not behind it. And the knees of his trousers were dirty and worn from digging. Then I saw that the bank was just behind the shop. When the League closed, I knew the tunnel was finished. And Saturday was the best day, because they would have two days to escape.”

“You reasoned it out beautifully,” I said.

“It saved me from boredom,” he answered with a yawn. “My life is one long effort to escape from the commonplaces of existence. These little problems help me to do so.”
